```{r setup, include=FALSE}
# Field context: Davletbakov (2026), Monitor Lizard_AD.docx;
# Davletbakov & Koshkin (2026), ENG_Golden Eagle_Methodological recommendations_AD.docx;
# Review of national methodologies.docx, sections 4 and 6, in ../slt_material.
# Tutorials informed by CREEM online-course modules 2, 3, 5, 6 and 8.
# All maps, survey records and numerical results are hypothetical/simulated.
# No source protocol is presented as an existing distance sampling design.
library(Distance)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,
                      fig.align = "center", dev = "pdf", fig.width = 6.5,
                      fig.height = 2.5, out.width = "85%",
                      fig.path = "figures/02-distance-", size = "footnotesize")
chunk_hook <- knitr::knit_hooks$get("chunk")
knitr::knit_hooks$set(chunk = function(x, options) {
  out <- chunk_hook(x, options)
  if (options$echo && options$size == "footnotesize")
    paste0("\n\\footnotesize\n\n", out, "\n\\normalsize\n") else out
})
bl <- rgb(0.16, 0.32, 0.75)
rd <- rgb(0.82, 0.1, 0.26)
grn <- rgb(0.55, 0.71, 0.0)
style_plot <- function(mfrow = c(1, 1)) {
  par(mfrow = mfrow, mar = c(3.5, 3.6, 1.5, 0.7),
      mgp = c(2.2, 0.65, 0), las = 1, bty = "l", cex = 0.9)
}
compact_results <- function(x, digits = 1) {
  knitr::kable(x[, c("Estimate", "lcl", "ucl", "cv")], digits = c(digits, digits, digits, 2),
               col.names = c("Estimate", "Lower 95% CI", "Upper 95% CI", "CV"),
               row.names = FALSE, format = "latex", booktabs = TRUE)
}
fmt <- function(x, digits = 1) format(round(x, digits), nsmall = digits, big.mark = ",")
preview_m <- read.csv("data/monitor_line_transects.csv")
preview_e <- read.csv("data/golden_eagle_point_transects.csv")
```

## Two hypothetical applications

\small

| | Desert monitor | Golden eagle |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Method | Walking line transects | Stationary point transects |
| Distance | Perpendicular to line | Radial from point |
| Main exercise | Full R walkthrough | Adapt the same workflow |
| Target | Available, above-ground animals | Available birds at a snapshot |

\vspace{0.2cm}
All records, maps and numerical results are **simulated teaching examples**.
They are not estimates for Kyrgyzstan, and the illustrated effort is not a recommendation.

We adapt parts of the current monitoring protocols; the distance sampling
surveys described here are hypothetical additions.

# Case study 1: Desert monitors

## Start with the existing monitor protocol

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
\small
The protocol combines:

- Visual routes through likely habitats, using a 20--30 m observation strip.

- Date, GPS, count, age, behaviour, habitat and photographs.

- Separate records of tracks and burrows.

:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth,height=0.48\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figures/desert-monitor-davletbakov.jpg}

\footnotesize Photo: A. Davletbakov
\end{center}
:::
::::

For distance sampling, add **representative lines, measured effort and distances**.

\footnotesize
Source: Davletbakov (2026).

## Define the population and the survey boundary

**Training question:** how many monitors are available above ground during
our standardised spring survey window?

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="57%"}
\small
- Map one hypothetical **100 km$^2$** region of southern foothill habitat.

- Define eligible animals, e.g. identifiable desert monitors of all ages.

- Choose comparable season, time and weather conditions.

- State that animals in refuges are outside this available-animal estimate.
:::
::: {.column width="43%"}
```{=latex}
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.62]
\fill[grn!12] (0,0) rectangle (5,5);
\draw[thick] (0,0) rectangle (5,5);
\node[align=center] at (2.5,2.5) {Hypothetical\\survey region\\100 km$^2$};
\draw[<->] (0,-0.4)--node[below,font=\small]{10 km}(5,-0.4);
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}
```
:::
::::

<!-- The protocol describes rare, fragmented southern occurrences, including
Batken and Fergana foothills. No actual site polygon or local density is claimed.
The conditional target requires standardised activity conditions and perfect
near-line detection among available animals; it is not all living monitors. -->

## Select lines before looking for animals

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="57%"}
\small
- Place lines randomly across the defined region.

- Include open and shrubby areas, including places with no known sightings.

- Plan access after selecting lines; do not move lines to promising tracks.

- Record inaccessible sections and revisit or apply a pre-agreed replacement rule.

**Teaching dataset:** 40 lines, each 2 km long. The diagram shows only a subset.
:::
::: {.column width="43%"}
```{=latex}
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.68]
\fill[grn!9] (0,0) rectangle (5,5);
\fill[grn!25] (3,0) rectangle (5,5);
\draw[thick] (0,0) rectangle (5,5);
\draw[gray,dashed] (0,0.7)..controls (1.5,2) and (2,0.3)..(5,2.5);
\foreach \x/\y in {0.3/4.2,2.3/4,3.9/3.2,0.5/2.3,2.2/2.4,3.6/1,1.1/0.4}{
\draw[bl,very thick] (\x,\y)--+(0.8,0);}
\node[font=\scriptsize] at (1.4,5.35) {Open};
\node[font=\scriptsize] at (4,5.35) {Shrubby};
\node[font=\scriptsize,align=center] at (2.5,-0.7) {Blue: selected lines\\Dashed: access track};
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}
```
:::
::::

<!-- Pure schematic, not generated GPS coordinates or the exact simulation design.
Random placement matches the introductory encounter-rate variance estimator.
Mapped habitat strata can be useful, but stratified estimation is not taught here. -->

## Pilot the method and standardise conditions

- Use a few lines spanning the habitat and visibility conditions.

- Check activity, near-line detection, distance accuracy and time per kilometre.

- Practise identification and first-position recording before the main survey.

- Record temperature, weather, start/end times and observers.

- Use pilot encounter rates and desired precision to plan the main effort.

For this exercise, search to **40 m on each side** and analyse distances
up to **30 m on each side**. These are illustrative choices to test in a pilot.

\alert{The protocol's strip width and our truncation distance are different quantities.}

<!-- Monitor protocol: spring/summer activity and reduced visibility while in
shelters; the methodology review adds morning/evening surveys outside peak heat.
Do not imply that these conditions guarantee every available animal is detected.
The document's 20--30 m strip is not silently reinterpreted as a half-width. -->

## Measure distance to the initial position

Search ahead while walking at a steady pace. Record the location where the
monitor was first detected, before approaching for a photograph.

```{=latex}
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[x=0.8cm,y=0.8cm]
\draw[->,very thick] (0,0)--(0,2.7) node[above,font=\small]{Line};
\fill (0,0) circle (0.07) node[left,font=\small]{Observer};
\fill[rd] (3.5,2) circle (0.09) node[right,font=\small]{Monitor};
\draw[dashed] (0,0)--node[below right,font=\small]{Sighting distance $r$}(3.5,2);
\draw[bl,thick] (0,2)--node[above,font=\small]{Perpendicular distance $x$}(3.5,2);
\draw (0,1.75)--(0.25,1.75)--(0.25,2);
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}
```

Record $x$ directly, or measure sighting distance and angle to the line.
For example, $r=20$ m and angle $30^\circ$ gives $x=20\sin(30^\circ)=10$ m.

<!-- Angle measured from the forward direction of the line, not compass north.
Use horizontal ground distance. Never measure the position reached after escape. -->

## Record sightings consistently

\small

| Survey record | Sighting record |
|:--|:--|
| Line ID, date and observers | Unique sighting ID and line ID |
| Start/end GPS and actual length | Initial position and perpendicular distance |
| Start/end time and conditions | Identification, age if reliable, behaviour |
| Habitat and completion status | Photograph reference and notes |

\vspace{0.2cm}
Count **one animal per sighting**, once during that pass. Do not create
additional detections when you photograph or follow it.

Keep uncertain identification for review. A missing distance for a sighting
is a missing data problem, not evidence of a zero count.

Before leaving, reconcile sightings and effort, resolve missing IDs or units,
and back up the sheet, photographs and GPS tracks.

## Keep effort, including lines with zero sightings

Record the **actual searched length**, even if no monitors are detected.
Do not use the planned length for an interrupted survey.

| Line | Actual length (km) | Detections | Status |
|:--|--:|--:|:--|
| M001 | 2.0 | 2 | Complete |
| M002 | 2.0 | 0 | Complete |
| M003 | 1.3 | 1 | Interrupted: weather |

Analyse only documented searched effort. Do not treat an unvisited line as a zero.

In the R teaching file, a completed line with no detections has its own row,
with `object` and `distance` left empty.

## Separate availability from distance detection

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="62%"}
A monitor underground may be missed even when its burrow is on the line.

\vspace{2em}

- Our curve corrects for **available animals overlooked at a distance**.

- It does not estimate how many monitors remained in refuges.

- Tracks and burrows provide useful separate evidence of presence.

- They are not extra monitor sightings in this analysis.

- Our analysis estimates abundance of \alert{available (above-ground)} animals.

:::
::: {.column width="38%"}

\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth,height=0.48\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figures/monitor-tracks-davletbakov.png}

\footnotesize Tracks: A. Davletbakov
\end{center}
:::
::::

<!-- Conventional g(0)=1 must hold for the conditional, available population.
The protocol's claims about converting indirect sign counts into population
size are not reproduced: a separate, validated relationship would be needed. -->

## Separate availability from distance detection

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="62%"}

- Our analysis estimates abundance of \alert{available (above-ground)} animals.

- Estimating \alert{all living} monitors requires additional information.

- Consider whether this is necessary to achieve monitoring goals.
:::
::: {.column width="38%"}

\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth,height=0.48\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figures/monitor-tracks-davletbakov.png}

\footnotesize Tracks: A. Davletbakov
\end{center}
:::
::::

\vspace{2em}

Distance to tracks and burrows can support **separate** distance sampling surveys, but these estimate the abundance of \alert{signs}. They should not be mixed with animal sighting data (unless using more advanced models).

<!-- Conventional g(0)=1 must hold for the conditional, available population.
The protocol's claims about converting indirect sign counts into population
size are not reproduced: a separate, validated relationship would be needed. -->

# Desert monitors: analysis in R

## Input data format

`monitor_line_transects.csv` captures survey information beside each detection.

\small

| Column | Meaning |
|:--|:--|
| `Region.Label`, `Area` | Region ID and area in km$^2$ |
| `Sample.Label`, `Effort` | Line ID and actual length in km |
| `object`, `distance` | Sighting ID and perpendicular distance in m |
| `habitat`, `status` | Visibility-related habitat and survey completion |

\vspace{0.1cm}
A zero-count line appears once, with missing `object` and `distance`.
A distance of **0 m** means a detected animal on the line, not a zero count.

<!-- Flat-file conventions: Distance::ds and flatfile documentation.
No size column: both examples count individuals, not groups. -->

## Import and inspect the data

```{r import-monitors, echo=TRUE}
library(Distance)
monitors <- read.csv("data/monitor_line_transects.csv")
monitors$habitat <- factor(monitors$habitat)
head(monitors[, c("Sample.Label", "Effort", "distance")], 4)
```

One row usually represents a detection; `nrow(monitors)` also includes
zero-count placeholders. Count sightings using `sum(!is.na(monitors$distance))`.

## Check the data and calculate effort

```{r check-monitors, echo=TRUE}
lines <- unique(monitors[, c("Sample.Label", "Effort")])
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(lines$Sample.Label))
stopifnot(all(lines$Effort > 0))
stopifnot(all(monitors$distance >= 0, na.rm = TRUE))
sum(lines$Effort)
sum(is.na(monitors$distance))
```

**Simulated data:** `r nrow(lines)` lines; `r sum(lines$Effort)` km searched;
`r sum(is.na(monitors$distance))` lines with no detections.

Sum effort **once per line**. `sum(monitors$Effort)` would count each line
again for every sighting. Keep the zero-count rows in the data supplied to `ds()`.

## Inspect distances and choose truncation

```{r monitor-histogram, echo=-1, fig.height=1.8}
style_plot()
w_monitor <- 30
hist(monitors$distance, breaks = seq(0, 40, 5),
     xlab = "Perpendicular distance (m)", main = "Simulated monitors",
     col = "lightblue")
abline(v = w_monitor, col = "red", lty = 2)
```

The red line marks the analysis limit, **30 m on each side**.
`r sum(monitors$distance > w_monitor, na.rm=TRUE)` sighting(s) lie beyond it.
`ds()` excludes those sightings while retaining line effort.

Choose the limit from measurement quality and the distance pattern; avoid
choosing it just to obtain a preferred abundance estimate.

## Reconcile metres, kilometres and square kilometres

```{r line-conversion, echo=TRUE}
line_units <- convert_units(
  "meter", "kilometer", "square kilometer")
```

\small

| Quantity | Unit in this exercise |
|:--|:--|
| Perpendicular distances and truncation | Metres |
| Actual line length | Kilometres |
| Region area | Square kilometres |
| Reported density | Available animals per km$^2$ |

\vspace{0.1cm}
Supply `line_units` to each model. Wrong units can produce a plausible-looking
curve but a badly wrong density estimate.

\footnotesize See https://distancesampling.org/Distance/reference/convert_units.html.

## Fit a simple half-normal model

```{r fit-monitor-hn, echo=TRUE, results='hide'}
monitor_hn <- ds(monitors,
  transect = "line", truncation = w_monitor,
  key = "hn", adjustment = NULL,
  convert_units = line_units, optimizer = "R")
```

- `"hn"` selects the half-normal curve.

- `adjustment = NULL` fits the basic shape without adjustment terms.

- Region area and effort in the file allow density and abundance estimation.

- `optimizer = "R"` uses the R fitting engine.

Use `summary(monitor_hn)` to inspect the full output.
We will select the important parts over the next slides.

\footnotesize
Workflow adapted from [distancesampling.org](https://distancesampling.org/online-course/02-detfns/R-prac/Pr2-instructions.html).

## Inspect the fitted detection curve

```{r plot-monitor-hn, echo=-1, fig.height=2.3}
style_plot()
plot(monitor_hn, showpoints = FALSE, nc = 6,
     xlab = "Perpendicular distance (m)")
```

```{r monitor-summary-values, include=FALSE}
monitor_summary <- summary(monitor_hn)
p_monitor <- monitor_summary$ds$average.p
```

**Simulated result:** average detection within 30 m is about
**`r fmt(100 * p_monitor, 0)`%** of available animals.

Check the near-line shoulder and the overall distance pattern. A good-looking
curve cannot establish that animals in burrows were available.

## Fit a plausible alternative

```{r fit-monitor-hr, echo=TRUE, results='hide'}
monitor_hr <- ds(monitors,
  transect = "line", truncation = w_monitor,
  key = "hr", adjustment = NULL,
  convert_units = line_units, optimizer = "R")
```

```{r compare-monitor-curves, fig.height=2.0, out.width='94%'}
style_plot(c(1, 2))
plot(monitor_hn, showpoints=FALSE, nc=6, main="Half-normal", xlab="Distance (m)")
plot(monitor_hr, showpoints=FALSE, nc=6, main="Hazard-rate", xlab="Distance (m)")
```

Both models use **the same data, effort and 30 m limit**.
Compare their fit and estimates; do not choose a curve just because it is flexible.

## Compare relative support using AIC

```{r monitor-aic, echo=TRUE}
AIC(monitor_hn, monitor_hr)
```

```{r aic-values, include=FALSE}
aic_simple <- AIC(monitor_hn, monitor_hr)
aic_gap <- abs(diff(aic_simple$AIC))
```

**Simulated result:** the AIC difference is **`r fmt(aic_gap)`**.
The half-normal has the lower AIC, but support is fairly similar.

AIC compares these candidates. It does not tell us whether either model is
adequate, or whether the field assumptions hold.

## Check goodness of fit

```{r monitor-gof, echo=-1, results='hide', fig.width=3, fig.height=3, out.width='38%'}
style_plot()
monitor_gof <- gof_ds(monitor_hn)
```

The Q--Q plot should stay reasonably close to the diagonal.
Simulated test p-value: **`r fmt(monitor_gof$dsgof$CvM$p, 2)`**.
A large p-value does not prove the model is correct.

Investigate systematic deviations, rounded distances, or a deficit near zero
before using the model for inference.

## Extract density and abundance

```{r monitor-estimates, echo=TRUE, results='hide'}
monitor_D <- monitor_hn$dht$individuals$D
monitor_N <- monitor_hn$dht$individuals$N
```

**Simulated available-animal density, per km$^2$:**

```{r monitor-density-table, results='asis'}
compact_results(monitor_D, 2)
```

**Simulated available-animal abundance in the 100 km$^2$ region:**

```{r monitor-abundance-table, results='asis'}
compact_results(monitor_N, 0)
```

`lcl` and `ucl` give lower and upper confidence limits. `cv` measures uncertainty
relative to the estimate; it is not detection probability.

## Interpret the uncertainty

```{r monitor-interval, fig.height=1.6}
style_plot()
plot(monitor_N$Estimate, 1, xlim = c(0, monitor_N$ucl * 1.1),
     ylim = c(0.7, 1.3), pch = 16, col = bl, yaxt = "n",
     xlab = "Simulated available-animal abundance", ylab = "")
segments(monitor_N$lcl, 1, monitor_N$ucl, 1, col = bl, lwd = 3)
points(monitor_N$Estimate, 1, pch = 16, col = bl, cex = 1.3)
```

Report approximately **`r fmt(monitor_N$Estimate, 0)` available monitors**,
with a 95% CI of **`r fmt(monitor_N$lcl, 0)`--`r fmt(monitor_N$ucl, 0)`**.

- Uncertainty includes encounter-rate variation and detection-model estimation.

- The interval does not include bias from unrepresentative lines or missed
  animals at zero distance.

- Wider intervals limit our ability to distinguish population changes.

## What would an uncorrected count suggest?

```{r uncorrected-density, echo=TRUE, results='hide'}
n_retained <- sum(monitors$distance <= w_monitor, na.rm = TRUE)
strip_km2 <- 2 * w_monitor / 1000 * sum(lines$Effort)
raw_density <- n_retained / strip_km2
```

```{r raw-corrected-plot, fig.height=1.8}
style_plot()
barplot(c(raw_density, monitor_D$Estimate),
        names.arg = c("Count / strip area", "Detection corrected"),
        col = c("grey65", bl), border = NA,
        ylab = "Available animals per km2", main = "Simulated monitors")
```

These use the **same retained sightings and surveyed strip**.
The model adds a correction for available animals overlooked during the search.

## Add one detection covariate

```{r fit-monitor-covariate, echo=TRUE, results='hide'}
monitor_cov <- ds(monitors,
  transect = "line", truncation = w_monitor,
  key = "hn", adjustment = NULL, formula = ~habitat,
  convert_units = line_units, optimizer = "R")
```

```{r covariate-comparison, echo=TRUE}
AIC(monitor_hn, monitor_cov)
```

**Result:** habitat improves AIC support. Note here it explains detection,
not a model of monitor abundance in each habitat.

Inspect this model's fit with `plot(monitor_cov)` and `gof_ds(monitor_cov)`.

<!-- In simulation true available density is the same in both habitats; only
half-normal scale differs. Pooled CDS illustrates approximate pooling robustness.
A covariate model is an introductory extension, not stratified abundance inference.
The half-normal remains the transparent main walkthrough, not claimed as final
best model after adding habitat. Companion code includes all candidate outputs. -->

# Case study 2: Golden eagles

## Start with the existing eagle protocol

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="56%"}
\small
The protocol searches potential nesting areas using regular observation stops.

- Stop spacing responds to valley width and terrain.

- Inspections last at least 5 minutes, often 15--30 minutes.

- Record birds, perches and nests separately.

- The sighting card already includes radial distance and azimuth.

:::
::: {.column width="44%"}
\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth,height=0.46\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figures/golden-eagle-davletbakov.jpg}

\footnotesize Photo: A. Davletbakov
\end{center}
:::
::::

Our DS addition uses **representative points and a bird snapshot**.

\footnotesize
Source: Davletbakov & Koshkin (2026)

## Define what the point survey estimates

**Research question:** what is the density of available golden eagles at a
standardised snapshot in a hypothetical **1,000 km$^2$** region?

- Count identifiable individual birds at that moment.

- This is not an estimate of occupied nests, breeding pairs or nesting success.

- Keep nest/perch records in the existing monitoring programme.

- An eagle hidden behind a ridge is not made detectable by recording a distance.

A regional estimate requires representative points **and** a defensible
available-animal detection model near zero distance.

<!-- No claim that standard point DS can recover total eagle density in rugged
Pamir-Alai terrain. Availability must be distinguished from declining detection
with distance; spatially biased visible sectors cannot simply represent hidden
sectors without additional design/model assumptions. -->

## Select points and assess the view

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="58%"}
- Select points across the target region before visiting known nests.

- Choose safe access without shifting points to the best-looking perches.

- Pilot how much of each circle is visible; map terrain obstructions.

- Avoid overlapping observation sessions and double recording the same bird.

:::
::: {.column width="42%"}
```{=latex}
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.6]
\fill[bl!5] (0,0) circle (2.3);
\draw[bl] (0,0) circle (2.3);
\fill[gray!40] (0,0)--(1.3,1.9) arc (56:135:2.3)--cycle;
\fill (0,0) circle (0.1);
\node[font=\small,align=center] at (0.1,1.4) {Blocked by\\ridge};
\node[font=\small,align=center] at (0,-1.2) {Visible sector};
\node[font=\scriptsize,align=center] at (0,-3) {A blocked circle is not\\a fully surveyed circle};
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}
```
:::
::::

\vspace{1em}

Our idealised exercise has **100 completed points** with unobstructed circles.
A real programme may need a different method where views are consistently restricted.

<!-- Sector shown schematically; no sector-area correction is taught. A
covariate or simply subtracting unseen area does not guarantee unbiased inference.
The data generator assumes ideal full-circle coverage. -->

## Use a snapshot, not an accumulating bird list

For the hypothetical pilot, use a consistent **2-minute settling period**,
then **5 minutes to locate birds**, followed by one designated snapshot.

```{=latex}
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[x=0.8cm,y=0.7cm,>=Stealth]
\draw[->,thick] (0,0)--(10,0);
\foreach \x/\txt in {0/Arrive,2/Begin locating,7/Snapshot} {
\draw (\x,0.12)--(\x,-0.12);
\node[below,font=\small,align=center] at (\x,-0.2) {\txt};}
\node[above,font=\small] at (1,0.1) {Settle};
\node[above,font=\small] at (4.5,0.1) {Locate birds};
\node[above,font=\small] at (8.5,0.1) {Confirm positions};
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}
```

Record each bird's position **at the snapshot**. Do not add birds arriving later.
Pilot this timing; it is not a validated golden eagle protocol.

Keep targeted nest inspections separate and follow the source protocol's
weather and nest-disturbance restrictions.

<!-- Snapshot approach: CREEM point-transect practical and field-method module;
2+5 minutes is an explicit hypothetical choice, not quoted from CREEM or the

## Record horizontal radial distance

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="63%"}
- Measure from the point to the bird's snapshot position, not its later perch.

- Use rangefinder/GPS and bearing to locate it; use **horizontal** distance.

- A sloping sightline or distance to a flying bird is not automatically ground distance.

- Search to 1,200 m for this exercise; analyse within a 1,000 m radius.

:::
::: {.column width="37%"}
```{=latex}
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.4]
\draw[bl] (0,0) circle (2.5);
\fill (0,0) circle (0.1) node[below,font=\small]{Point};
\fill[rd] (1.4,1.5) circle (0.1) node[above,font=\scriptsize]{Bird};
\draw[->,thick] (0,0)--node[above left,font=\scriptsize]{Radial distance}(1.4,1.5);
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}
```
:::
::::

\vspace{2em}

Large, fast-moving birds require careful position recording. If snapshot
locations cannot be obtained reliably, revise the method before collecting main data.

## Keep point effort and individual sightings

\small

| Survey record | Sighting record |
|:--|:--|
| Point ID and GPS, date, observers | Unique bird ID linked to point |
| Timing, completion, visibility and weather | Snapshot radial distance and azimuth |
| One completed snapshot: `Effort = 1` | Identification, behaviour, photograph |

\vspace{0.2cm}

\normalsize 
An empty completed point contributes effort and a zero-count placeholder.
A missed or aborted point is not an empty completed point.

Effort is **the number of completed snapshots**, not observation minutes.
For later repeat surveys, retain point and visit IDs and account for dependence;
do not pool revisits as independent new points.

## Import the point data and inspect distances

```{r import-eagles, echo=-1, fig.height=1.7}
style_plot()
eagles <- read.csv("data/golden_eagle_point_transects.csv")
points <- unique(eagles[, c("Sample.Label", "Effort")])
stopifnot(nrow(points) == 100, all(points$Effort == 1))
hist(eagles$distance, breaks = seq(0, 1200, 150),
     xlab = "Radial distance (m)", main = "Simulated eagles",
     col = "lightblue")
```

Counts can rise before falling: **outer rings have more area**.
This histogram is not a graph of detection probability.

`r sum(is.na(eagles$distance))` completed points have no detections;
retain those rows when fitting the model.

## Fit the point model and plot both views

```{r fit-eagle, echo=TRUE, results='hide'}
point_units <- convert_units("meter", NULL, "square kilometer")
w_eagle <- 1000
eagle_hn <- ds(eagles, transect = "point",
  truncation = w_eagle, key = "hn", adjustment = NULL,
  convert_units = point_units, optimizer = "R")
```

```{r eagle-two-views, fig.height=2.3, out.width='94%'}
style_plot(c(1, 2))
plot(eagle_hn, showpoints = FALSE, main = "Detection probability")
par(mar = c(3.5, 6, 1.5, 0.7))
plot(eagle_hn, pdf = TRUE, showpoints = FALSE, ylab = "",
     main = "Observed distance distribution")
mtext("Probability density", side = 2, line = 4.3, las = 0)
```

`plot(eagle_hn, pdf = TRUE)` combines ring area and detection: its peak
can occur away from zero. Bars show scaled frequencies; only the left
curve is detection probability.

## Check and interpret the eagle result

```{r eagle-results, echo=TRUE, results='hide'}
eagle_gof <- gof_ds(eagle_hn, plot = FALSE)
eagle_D <- eagle_hn$dht$individuals$D
eagle_N <- eagle_hn$dht$individuals$N
```

**Simulated available-bird density per km$^2$:**

```{r eagle-density-table, results='asis'}
compact_results(eagle_D, 3)
```

**Simulated abundance in the hypothetical region:** approximately
**`r fmt(eagle_N$Estimate, 0)` birds**, 95% CI
**`r fmt(eagle_N$lcl, 0)`--`r fmt(eagle_N$ucl, 0)`**.

Inspect the Q--Q plot using `gof_ds(eagle_hn)`. As with monitors, compare plausible
alternatives before choosing a final model.

\alert{These are available-bird snapshot estimates, not total eagle population or
nesting-territory estimates.}

## Plan comparable surveys through time

- Retain the same sampling design and target region.

- Repeat within a comparable season, time window and activity conditions.

- Record habitat, visibility, observer and effort changes every year.

- Estimate detection for the new data; do not assume it stayed constant.

- Report uncertainty and changes in the available-animal estimate.

**Fewer active monitors or visible eagles can reflect changed availability.**
A trend in these estimates becomes a total-population trend only with
additional evidence that availability is comparable or has been accounted for.

## Report the estimate and the survey it describes

A useful report states:

- Species, region, dates and **available-animal target**.

- Sampling design, number of completed surveys and actual effort.

- Distances, units, truncation and detection model, with checks.

- Density/abundance, confidence interval and limitations.
